name: Hebrew
blurb: Hebrew is written from right to left with 22 letters, all of them consonants; the vowels were added later as dots and dashes (niqqud).

scripts.label: Square script
scripts.about: The “square” letters, taken over from the Aramaic script after the Babylonian exile (6th century BCE) and still used today.
scripts.note: Type as it sounds: sh for ש, ch for ח, ts for צ, ' for א and ` for ע. Short a and e inside a word are left out; i becomes י and o or u become ו, as in many Hebrew spellings; final letters (ך ם ן ף ץ) appear by themselves. The line under the letters spells out what is written.
groups: alef · silent, or a catch in the throat
vav · v (anciently w); also o and u
ayin · a sound from deep in the throat
final kaf · kaf at the end of a word
final mem · mem at the end of a word
final nun · nun at the end of a word
final pe · pe at the end of a word
final tsadi · tsadi at the end of a word
marks: sheva · a short e, or no vowel
dagesh · a doubled or hard letter
samples: Shalom: peace, and also hello and goodbye
Tikkun olam: “repairing the world”, a phrase found in the Mishnah
Bereshit: “in the beginning”, the first word of the Bible and the Hebrew name of Genesis

scripts.label: Paleo-Hebrew
scripts.about: The older Hebrew letters, close to the Phoenician alphabet, used by the kingdoms of Israel and Judah from about the 10th century BCE.
scripts.note: The same letters in their older shapes, with no final forms and a dot between words, as on the Siloam inscription. Type as for Hebrew: sh, ch, ts, ' and `.
groups: alef · silent, or a catch in the throat
waw · w; also o and u
ayin · a sound from deep in the throat
samples: “And this was the matter of the tunnel”: the Siloam inscription, cut in Hezekiah’s tunnel in Jerusalem around 700 BCE
